Chasles Tangents

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Move dots around a circle and watch four lines that just touch it.
How to play: Drag a blue dot around the circle, or drag the small grey dots to move or resize the circle. Focus a dot and use the arrow keys, and press Show names or Allow hint to see more.
Look for the math

Four lines that just touch a circle can meet one more touching line in four places. Those four places carry a number that stays the same when you move a fifth dot anywhere on the circle. That is the surprise behind this picture.

Four touches, four points

The circle is a conic. The line touching it at T is fixed; call it t. Touch the circle at A, B, C and D and those four tangents cut t at A', B', C' and D'. Read their positions along t to get the cross-ratio (A'B'C'D') = ((c-a)/(c-b)) / ((d-a)/(d-b)), using signed distances along that line.

Chasles' theorem

Now draw the four lines from any other point K of the circle to A, B, C and D. They form a pencil, and its cross-ratio K(ABCD) is made from the signed sines of the angles between the lines. The applet's page claims K(ABCD) = (A'B'C'D'). That is Chasles' theorem: the number does not depend on where K sits. Move K and the number under the picture stays put.

A step that needs care

The page quotes Eves' short proof: ∠A'OT = ½∠AOT = ∠AKT. The first equality always holds, but the page's own Note warns that the second one does not. An inscribed angle at K is half the central angle only while K is on one arc from A to T; on the other arc it is the supplement, a half turn larger. Press Allow hint to watch the two angles. The cross-ratio is unchanged by that supplement, so the theorem survives even though this one line of the proof needs mending.

Checked, not just claimed

The logic test builds 240 different circles and point arrangements, and checks K(ABCD) = (A'B'C'D') at K and at twelve other places on each circle. It measures the two cross-ratios independently, checks that the angle step at O always holds and that the step at K holds on one arc but not the other, and compares every constructed point with a second transcription of the applet's own tangent and intersection bytecode.

Try dragging K slowly all the way around the circle with the hint on. The blue angle jumps by a half turn when K passes A or T, but the number below never changes.
